text: First day on the job. Your temporary pass won’t open the turnstile, the guard went for coffee, and the welcome meeting starts at 9:00. What now?
Your mentor greets you with: “I’ve only been here two weeks myself, but we’ll figure it out.” He’s holding your contract upside down.
HR hands you a welcome pack: a mug, a notebook and a thick brochure called “Our Values.” There’s an oral quiz on it in an hour. Read it?
The onboarding course on the intranet: 47 video lessons, 20 minutes each. The “Next” button only unlocks once the video ends.
Rita from the next department whispers an offer: “a tour of the office’s unwritten rules.” She says it’ll take five minutes. Sounds like an hour at least.
You’ve been added to the department chat. 312 unread messages, and everyone’s waiting for you to introduce yourself. Say something?
End of day one. You still don’t know where the bathroom is on this floor, and it’s getting awkward to ask. Admit it?
Your laptop is “still on its way.” The sysadmin gives you an ancient PC with the previous owner’s Solitaire still open — high score 1,200.
Your manager says to “read the documentation for now.” There is no documentation — just a folder called “New Folder (3)” with one screenshot.
Mom calls in the evening: “So, have they promoted you yet?” So far all you’ve got is a badge with your name misspelled.
First week of probation. 8:40 a.m.: the office is empty, lights off, nobody around. Looks like everyone here rolls in at eleven.
left: Sit in the dark and wait
right: Go for a walk till ten

text: Your mentor gives you a task: “Do it like last time.” It’s your third day. There was no last time. Ask?
Accounting needs a form for your payroll card. It’s eight pages long and asks for “paternal grandmother’s maiden name.”
Timur invites the newbies to a “get-to-know-you” at a bar after work. You don’t know anyone’s name yet, and your report to your mentor is due at nine tomorrow.
left: Go and get to know people

text: The office manager shows you your workspace: a desk by the meeting room door, a chair missing an armrest and a cactus “from the last person.” Thoughts?
left: Accept it all with a smile

text: HR sent an email about you to the whole company: photo, hobbies and the line “loves pies.” Now everyone walking by makes a pie joke.
You notice everyone on probation leaves at 6:00 sharp — except you. Apparently waiting for the boss to leave isn’t required.
The sysadmin hands you twelve passwords for different systems and asks you to “never write them down.” Each one expires in thirty days.
At the planning meeting the department head asks: “What does our newbie think?” Everyone turns to you. You’ve been here four days.
Olesya offers, “as a friend,” to share all her tasks “so you get up to speed faster.” She has thirty-eight of them.
In the newbie chat someone writes: “Does anyone else feel cheated about the cookies?” The cookies you were promised really aren’t in the kitchen.
right: Stay quiet, keep a low profile

text: HR asks you to fill out an “adaptation survey”: rate how happy you are on day three, from 1 to 10. It’s not anonymous.
Your mentor sends a 140-page handbook: “Just the important stuff.” The important parts are highlighted in yellow. Everything is highlighted in yellow.
At home you realize you’ve introduced yourself wrong all day: there are already two people with your name, so they listed you under a third variation.
Your first rush-hour commute. At the transfer the crowd sweeps you out the wrong exit. Seven minutes until the workday starts.
Your mentor leaves on a three-week vacation two days after you start. His parting words: “Message me if anything comes up. I won’t reply.”
The company portal demands a profile photo. The only decent one is from your graduation — wearing a crown.
right: Take a selfie against a wall

text: First Friday evening. You still don’t get what your department actually does, but nobody seems to care.
The guard demands to see your pass, though he saw you yesterday and the day before. Your pass is in your other jacket.
HR lost the copy of your diploma. They need the original, and it’s at your parents’ place in another city.
left: Ask your parents to mail it

text: Gosha kindly warns you that your desk is “cursed”: the last three people who sat there didn’t pass probation.
right: Hang a lucky charm on it

text: 64 emails in the morning. Half are department newsletters you didn’t know existed; the rest are automatic notifications about your own onboarding.
Your manager praises you in front of everyone for your first task. Truth is, your desk neighbor did almost all of it.
Your pass opens every floor except yours. Every time you have to wait for someone to come out.
Your mentor suggests a video “sync-up” at 8 p.m., since he’s in meetings all day. Your evening is already planned.
You showed up in a dress shirt; everyone else is in hoodies. Even the CEO is in a hoodie. You feel like a guest at the wrong wedding.
right: Run out and buy a hoodie

text: Vika asks how much salary you were offered. She says it’s “just for statistics” and already has a spreadsheet open.
On his way out the department head says: “Tomorrow, show me what you got done this week.” The week was mostly access requests.
A note on your monitor from the previous employee: “Don’t trust Sergei from logistics.” Sergei from logistics just emailed you.
right: Peel it off and forget it

text: Your mentor accidentally sends you a voice message meant for his wife: “The newbie seems okay, but slow.” You both pretend it never happened.
You accidentally put a fire emoji on a message about a colleague leaving the company. You can’t undo it — someone already noticed.
Halfway through probation. HR invites you to a “check-in chat” on Friday at 6:30 p.m. Saying no doesn’t seem to be an option.
Denis offers you his “lucky” chair: the last newbie who sat on it got promoted within a month. It creaks and leans to the left.
You need to sign twenty documents. HR says “don’t read them, it’s standard.” One is titled “Consent to Everything.”
At the meeting you hear “sync,” “sign-off,” “escalate,” “commit.” The only word you understand is “lunch.”
Your friends in the group chat ask about the new job and expect funny stories. The funniest thing all week: you got stuck in the turnstile.
Turns out it’s tradition for the newbie to bring a cake at the end of week one. You find this out on Friday morning.
Your manager asks why you still aren’t on the work messenger. You requested access a week ago; the ticket is “in progress.”
Lyova from the next department learns you’re new and cheerfully says: “Fresh blood! You’ll take the meeting minutes.” Nobody likes taking minutes.
First week done. You have seven new passwords, three mysterious tasks and one logo mug. Celebrate?
The printer on your floor glows red: “Paper jam in tray 4.” It has three trays. You need the contract printed in ten minutes.
You sent two pages to print, and the printer is now on page 100 of someone else’s presentation. Your pages are at the back of the queue.
6:55 p.m. The printer finally prints your report, but every page has a streak and a “Low toner” message. Redo it?
The scanner emails every file to someone who quit two years ago. The settings are password-protected and nobody knows the password.
The office manager trusted you to laminate the “Quiet Please” signs. The laminator chewed up the first one and smells of burning plastic.
You’re shredding old drafts when the shredder suddenly grabs the end of your tie. Your manager is walking past.
Your open-space neighbor plays voice messages on speaker every morning. Today his aunt is sharing her recipe for meat jelly.
The colleague across from you loudly crunches a carrot during your call with a client. The client asks what that noise is.
Every evening someone switches off the lights at 6:01 without checking if anyone’s still there. Tonight you’re left in the dark.
New open-space rule: “Quiet hours from 10 to 12.” Your keyboard clicks like castanets, and people have turned around twice.
Your neighbor put a “Pumpkin Spice” scented candle on the shared desk. By lunch your eyes are watering, but everyone else loves it.
Before leaving you notice someone left their backpack on your chair and half a cup of tea on your desk. Looks like your spot’s been “reserved.”
The coffee machine asks: “What’s your favorite drink?” and offers to create a fingerprint profile. The line behind you sighs.
The coffee machine only makes cappuccino: the “Americano” button is worn off, and someone drew a skull there in marker. Press the skull?
In the evening the coffee machine decided to self-clean and flooded the counter with hot water. Someone’s papers were lying there.
Your first time using the office coffee machine. You press a button — it hums, blinks and produces only steam. People behind you whisper.
The office manager announces: coffee is now by coupon only, five cups a week. You drink five cups by lunch.
The coffee machine gets turned off after six, and you have two hours of report left. There’s a “rainy day” pack of instant coffee in the cupboard.
Someone ate your yogurt from the office fridge. The lid had a sticker with your name; the empty cup has lipstick marks.
The office manager threatens to throw out everything in the fridge on Friday. Your soup container is in there — forgotten two weeks ago.
The kitchen fridge emits a smell you can detect from the elevator. Someone has to open it. Everyone’s looking at you, the newbie.
There’s a fridge-cleaning rota on the door. Your name is down for this Friday, though nobody asked you.
The microwave line is eight people long, each with a container. Your break is only half an hour.
Someone microwaved fish, and the whole kitchen smells like the sea. You’re the last person leaving the kitchen just as the CEO walks in.
The office kettle switches off a second before boiling, then starts heating again. This has been going on for twenty minutes.
You emptied the water cooler, so etiquette says you’re the one installing the new 5-gallon jug. Someone’s already waiting with a mug.
The kitchen sink is piled with dirty mugs. Yours is somewhere at the bottom. Everyone else has gone home.
Fridays are casual here, but you came in a suit. You have a lunch meeting with an important client, and everyone else is in jeans.
HR reminds everyone of the dress code: “No sneakers.” You’re in sneakers; your dress shoes are at home. Website photo shoot in an hour.
In the evening you discover you wore your sweater inside out all day. The tag was sticking out on your back. Nobody said a word.
The chat announced Bright Socks Week. Your socks come in gray, black and more gray. You leave the house in ten minutes.
You and the department head are wearing the same shirt. He noticed too and says: “Well, that’s it — we’re a team now.”
The dress code for the office party is “Glamorous Office.” You own one blazer and some glitter from a card-making kit.
Your bus drove right past the stop again without stopping. The next one is in twenty minutes; a taxi is pricey.
Your lunchtime doctor’s appointment ran long, and now your minibus is stuck in traffic. Meeting in fifteen minutes.
The evening train is canceled. The next one’s in an hour, and dinner is waiting at home. A colleague offers a ride, but he lives the other way.
You run into the department head on the subway. Seven more stops together, and zero topics to talk about.
On your way to a client meeting you realize you took the minibus in the wrong direction. You only figured it out at the last stop.
On the evening subway, the woman next to you is reading a book you’ve wanted for ages. She’s on the last page, it seems. This is your stop.
Your alarm didn’t go off; you wake up at 9:10. The workday started at nine. You’re on probation.
You’re twenty minutes late back from lunch: the cafe forgot your order. Your manager pointedly checks the clock.
You arrive at the company dinner an hour after everyone else. All that’s left are empty plates and coworkers already doing karaoke.
You walk into the building at 9:00 sharp, but the elevator reaches your floor at 9:04. The planning meeting has already started.
Coworkers invite you to the cafeteria for lunch. You brought food from home, but eating alone in the kitchen is boring.
You paid for the whole department’s lunch because “we’ll send you the money later.” A week later, two out of seven have paid.
At 9 a.m. your coworkers are already debating where to go for lunch. The chat poll has dragged on for forty minutes and 120 messages.
At lunch coworkers discuss who’s the slowest in the department. You’ve been here a week and suspect they’re about to mention you.
right: Make a joke about it first

text: Coworkers plan a “long lunch” on Friday from 1 to 4. Your manager’s on vacation, but you’re still on probation.
Your desk is right by the entrance, and everyone who walks in feels the need to nod, say hi or ask for directions.
Your desk neighbor keeps moving your chair over to his desk because “it’s comfier.” Today he took your monitor too.
Your mentor texts at 7:30 a.m.: “Look over my code before the meeting, it’s all self-explanatory.” The file is 3,000 lines with zero comments.
Your mentor is an hour late, and you can’t start a single task without him. The department is giving you pitying looks.
left: Ask the neighbors for a task

text: Your mentor teaches you “real work”: how to keep a work file open whenever management walks behind you.
A calendar reminder pops up: “30 days left of probation.” One of your coworkers set it up as a joke.
Your boss asks you to run the morning stand-up “to test your leadership skills.” It starts in fifteen minutes.
left: Run it as best you can

text: The man across from you on the subway is reading a printout with your company’s logo. He might be your future client.
You decided to ride a rental scooter to work. Halfway there the battery died, and the office is two more kilometers uphill.
The morning bus driver is blasting accordion music. The whole bus is silently humming along. You forgot your headphones.
You fell asleep on the train and woke up to the conductor shaking your shoulder. You’ve overshot your station by three stops.
You biked to work and discovered the office has no shower. At 10:00 you have a face-to-face with the department head.
You’re ten minutes late, and the CEO is standing by the elevator. He’s late too, and gives you a conspiratorial wink.
Late again — third time this week. A coworker quietly advises: “Say you were held up at the doctor’s. Everyone does.”
In the coffee line you end up behind the division director. He’s been choosing a drink for two minutes, reading the ingredients.
Coworkers are chipping in for a coffee bean subscription, $10 a month each. You only drink tea.
left: Chip in to be a team player

text: A new note on the fridge: “Whoever’s eating other people’s cheesecakes — the camera sees you.” Yesterday you took one from a box marked “for everyone.”
You head to the kitchen first thing, and the office manager is already there with gloves and a trash bag: “Great, help me clear out the cupboards.”
right: Say you have an urgent call

text: You got a desk right by the window. The sun hits your monitor so hard all you can see is your own reflection.
The printer greets you with: “Firmware update required. Do not turn off the device.” The update has been running for three days.
You accidentally printed a personal document — your résumé for another company. It’s sitting in the shared printer tray. HR is standing right there.
The color printer is available only “with manager approval.” You need to print one chart for a presentation.
The meeting-room projector shows everything mirrored. Your manager asks you to “fix it quick” — you’re the young generation, after all.
Your wireless mouse suddenly starts controlling the cursor on your neighbor’s computer. He’s already sent someone a spreadsheet twice.
The landline on your desk is ringing, and you don’t know how to transfer calls. Judging by the number, it’s the CEO.
Coworkers are going for the business lunch at “the usual place.” All they serve is soup with a lone floating circle of grease and fruit punch.
At a team lunch the department head tells a joke you heard in kindergarten. Everyone laughs a little louder than necessary.
Coworkers argue over who pays the shared bill. They propose “last one to finish pays.” You’re a slow eater.
There’s a cake in the fridge reading “Happy Birthday, Marina!” Marina works in another building. The cake is three days old.
In the kitchen you accidentally broke someone’s mug that says “World’s Best Grandma.” No witnesses except the coffee machine.
A coworker is filming a “day in the life of an office” video for social media right in the open space. Your desk, piled with candy wrappers, is in the shot.
Open-space debate: open the window or not? Half are freezing, half are suffocating. You sit right by the window.
The client meeting was moved to your office in thirty minutes. Your T-shirt says “Don’t Talk to Me Before Coffee.”
Documents need delivering, but the courier is sick. Your manager asks you to take the subway to the other end of town.
Your mentor suggests “a quick work session” on the weekend so you can settle in better. You planned to do absolutely nothing.
Before leaving, your mentor leaves a note: “I’m out tomorrow, you’ve got this.” Below it: a smiley face and three exclamation marks.
A coworker confides that the boss “keeps an eye on” newbies based on who leaves last. It’s 6:05 p.m.
You’re asked to sign a one-month probation extension, “just a formality.” No reason given.
On the evening train you run into a coworker from accounting. She happily sits next to you and starts telling you about her vacation. It’s an hour’s ride.
You barely squeezed into a rush-hour subway car. Your backpack is still outside, stuck in the doors. The train isn’t moving.
You called a taxi after work, and the driver turns out to be a former employee of your company. He spends the whole ride explaining why he quit.
You decided to walk home to clear your head. Twenty minutes later you realize you’re lost in an industrial zone.
right: Trust the GPS to the end

text: You missed the start of the evening team-building event, and all the teams are set. The host offers you the role of judge.
The office manager asked you to switch off the coffee machine before leaving. In the morning it turns out she meant the kitchen lights.
Before the holidays the office manager announces: anything left in the fridge after 7 p.m. gets thrown out. Your expensive cheese is in there.
On your way out you notice the kitchen faucet is leaking, and a plumber can only be called through a ticket in the system.
Coworkers invite you to a late “lunch-dinner” after six since they didn’t make it earlier. Mentally you went home hours ago.
Only you and the cleaner are left in the open space. He’s running the vacuum right by your desk and isn’t moving on.
In the evening HR announces: tomorrow is the company calendar photo shoot, everyone wear white. You have nothing white.
You stayed late to print a report, but the printer demands a personal PIN. You’ll get your PIN in a week.
right: Send the report as a file

text: On your way out you realize the key to your locker is stuck in the lock. Your jacket is inside, and it’s raining.
In the evening you replay everything you said today. Especially: “Sure, I’ll figure it out tonight.”
The alarm went off, but you hit “Stop” instead of “Snooze.” It’s 8:20; you needed to leave at 8:00.
The cat lay down on the shirt you ironed for your first team meeting. It’s now covered in fur, and time is short.
left: Lint-roll it with tape in the elevator

text: Your roommate has hogged the bathroom for forty minutes. You have to leave in twenty and haven’t even washed your face.
The navigation app routes you through a closed subway station. The alternative: three transfers and a bus through back streets.
The tram conductor won’t take cards, only cash. All you have is a card and a few coins to last until payday.
The minibus driver asks passengers to pass the fare forward. You do, and a minute later you’re handed change for twelve people and asked to distribute it.
right: Pass it back to the driver

text: The barista at the cafe near the office knows your name and order. Today he ceremoniously hands you “the usual,” though you wanted to try something new.
In the morning the cleaner is mopping right by your desk and asks you not to walk there until it dries. That’ll be about twenty minutes.
The guard at the entrance is a huge soccer fan and expects you to discuss last night’s match. You didn’t watch and don’t know who played.
An intern who started a week after you already treats you as an “old-timer” and asks questions you can’t answer.
You’re in the elevator with the CEO. He asks: “And who are you?” Eight more floors to go.
The work messenger on your phone starts pinging at 6 a.m.: coworkers in another time zone are already at work.
The facilities manager issues stationery strictly by the list: two pens, one notepad, five paper clips a month. You ask for a stapler.
Your open-space neighbor shakes your hand every morning. Only his hands are always cold and a bit sticky.
A sign on the coffee machine: “Broken. Do not touch!” Next to it, a coworker with a mug says he knows a secret trick.
A foreign delegation is visiting today. Word is everyone must look “respectable.” You’re wearing dinosaur sneakers.
You’re late because you helped an elderly lady carry her bags to her door. Your manager probably won’t appreciate it.
The vending machine ate your last two dollars and didn’t drop the chocolate bar. It’s dangling from the coil, half out.
At the cafeteria counter you’re accidentally given a double portion of meatballs. The cook has already turned away. Coworkers are behind you in line.
You ordered lunch to the office, but the courier took it to the building next door with the same number. He’s waiting for you there.
A vegan coworker offers you a taste of his lunch: a lentil patty. He’s watching expectantly, napkin at the ready.
You bring homemade borscht in a thermos for lunch. Coworkers have caught the scent and are drifting toward the kitchen with spoons.
The boss suggests having lunch together to “get to know each other better.” It’s at a restaurant, and the bill will apparently be split.
Your mouse jerks across the desk: there’s a torn-off corner of an “Inventory No. 0045” sticker under it. Without the sticker, the mouse might get written off.
The letter “J” doesn’t work on your keyboard. You’re writing a report on the “Jade Jewel Junction” housing complex.
You got a second monitor. It glows blue even when turned off and crackles quietly now and then.
You answered the landline, and it’s an elderly lady who thinks she’s calling her doctor’s office. She really needs advice.
The department printer prints everything on the back of used paper — “to save money.” The back of your report has someone’s salaries on it.
After the meeting you realize you walked off with someone’s expensive pen. The owner is already searching every desk.
You mixed up chats and sent a dancing cat sticker to the work chat. The boss reacts with a “?”
Coworkers in the open space are celebrating someone’s birthday: balloons, party poppers, singing. You’re on an important call with a client.
right: Invite the client to sing along

text: The coworker across from you sneezes loudly every five minutes and says “Sorry,” and everyone chants “Bless you.” Hard to work.
The open space now has “quiet zones” and “social zones.” Your desk suddenly ended up in a social zone, and you love quiet.
You get your first solo assignment, with the note: “It’s important, but don’t panic.” Deadline: today at 5 p.m.
Your mentor assigns you a task and then immediately does it himself “because it’s faster.” You watch him type.
On the train home you dozed off on a stranger’s shoulder. He hasn’t woken you for five stations and is patiently reading the news.
You’re riding home in a coworker’s car. In traffic he puts on an audiobook about leveling up your leadership skills. An hour to go.
You’re racing to the train on a scooter in the evening when you spot your boss behind you on an identical scooter. He’s late for the train too.
You missed the last bus to your neighborhood. The next one’s in the morning. A coworker lives near the office.
You discover someone’s been sipping your milk every day. Today there’s a smiley face drawn on the carton.
After the office party there’s a mountain of dishes in the kitchen. The office manager suggests that “whoever’s still here” wash them. You’re still here.
In the evening you volunteered to clean the coffee machine and found something green growing inside. It seems to be moving.
left: Scrub it and save the coffee
right: Take a photo for the chat

text: Mom calls to ask if they feed you well at work. You’re finishing your second chocolate bar instead of dinner.
A college classmate invites you to a bar, bragging he’s already been promoted. You just left a meeting about how to use the printer.
Your mentor gives you a ride to the subway and offers “advice for life”: never say “that’s not my job.”
In the last week of probation you’re asked to stay after work and “just have a chat” with HR. No details.
You’re the last to leave and notice someone left their computer on with a chat open. They’re discussing you.
You decide to wear your favorite bright shirt tomorrow. Your roommate says: “You can’t wear that to an office.” Your office is dull.
You’ve been told to shred old documents. There are six boxes, and the shredder overheats every ten minutes.
Lying in bed, you remember calling a coworker by the wrong name in the kitchen today. She corrected you, and you made the same mistake again.
Anya brings a mug to your desk that says “Newbie of the Month.” Turns out every newbie gets one, and drinking from it at stand-up is mandatory.
Stepan insists the best way to fit in is to bring cookies to the kitchen every morning. He’s very fond of oatmeal ones, by the way.
At 9:05 Nina loudly announces: “Whoever took my stapler — give it back!” Her stapler is on your desk, and you have no idea how it got there.
The group lead wants a daily report from you on “what you did yesterday.” Yesterday you mostly filed access requests.
The CEO’s assistant asks you to help “for a sec” carry boxes of partner gifts to the sixth floor. The elevator’s broken.
Boris comes in at 7:00 and leaves at 4:00. Now he insists you join his “early birds club.” You’re a night owl.
A courier brought a package addressed to your predecessor. Judging by the sound, there’s something glass and sloshing inside.
The office manager asks every newbie to post “three interesting facts about yourself” in the team chat. So far everyone wrote about travel and cats.
A poll in the team chat: “What time are we leaving for the cleanup day tomorrow?” It’s news to you that you’re part of a cleanup day.
The tram has stopped: a car is parked on the tracks. Passengers debate who’ll go find the driver. Everyone looks at you.
You were so afraid of being late that you reached the office at 7:30. The doors open at 8:30, and it’s drizzling.
In the morning subway crush someone spilled coffee on you. There’s a stain the size of Australia on your shirt.
right: Button your jacket to the chin

text: You’re told you can’t take time off during probation. And today at 10:00 a repairman is coming to fix your fridge.
Arseny brings his own coffee machine to the office and announces it’s “insiders only.” You don’t know yet if you’re an insider.
The sysadmin asks you to come in at 8 a.m. tomorrow to install software. He himself works from eight to four.
Your desk is pushed right up against a coworker’s, and every half hour he moves your monitor “to his half.”
The sales folks hint that your cat socks are “not very professional.” You notice two of them are wearing shark socks.
Sveta asks you to look after her ficus while she’s on vacation: water it, wipe the leaves and “talk to it kindly.”
At lunch Sasha says he’s switched jobs five times this year and “it was awful everywhere.” You’ve never switched jobs.
right: Change the topic to TV shows

text: The department head asks you to speak at the all-hands about “My First Month.” Five minutes, two hundred people.
The cafeteria offers a “$5 set lunch”: soup, main course, fruit punch and a mandatory slice of bread with mustard.
Coworkers lunch at a cafe where the waiter always brings the wrong thing. Today you got fish instead of chicken.
Ilya comes over: “Hey, you have database access, right? Look up one number for me.” You were given access for a different task.
You find your lunch container in the fridge, and next to it an identical one, also labeled with your name. There are two of you with the same name.
Coworkers are arguing in the kitchen over whose turn it is to buy dish sponges. The office manager asks you, the newbie, to “sort it out.”
Instead of coffee, the machine gave you hot milk that smells of cocoa. It has no “milk” or “cocoa” buttons.
You’re trying to print one page, and the printer says “Printing 1 of 238.” Someone apparently sent an entire book.
You’ve been asked to scan a 200-page contract. The scanner takes one page at a time and asks “Continue?” every time.
Your open-space neighbors are discussing you: “What’s the name of the one by the window?” You’re three feet away, hidden by the water cooler.
A coworker in the next row has been humming the same line of a song all morning. Now it’s stuck in your head.
Your manager says in passing: “Come see me after lunch.” Nothing else. Lunch starts in five minutes.
You were late to your own first presentation to the department: you mixed up the meeting rooms. Everyone’s waiting, the projector’s warmed up.
Badge photos were announced out of nowhere. Today your T-shirt says “Mondays Are the Worst,” and it’s Wednesday.
Before leaving, Marat proposes a bet: whoever finishes their report first skips kitchen duty for a week. Your report is five pages.
Vera asks you to cover her evening phone shift: “I have a date, pretty please.” You’d planned yoga.
At 6:10 p.m. the department head asks you to “run through” a spreadsheet. It has 4,000 rows and needs “fresh eyes.”
Coworkers invite you to their Wednesday board game night. The rules take forty minutes to explain.
In the evening team chat, coworkers argue whose turn it is to order water for the office. You’ve been tagged three times.
Your roommate invited guests, and you have a check-in with your mentor at eight tomorrow. The music is shaking the floor.
On the evening bus you recognize the man next to you as a future client discussed at today’s meeting. He doesn’t know you.
The evening minibus is packed, and the driver says: “Squeeze in, there’s standing room.” You’re already standing on one leg.
You got so absorbed in a task that you’re late for drinks with friends celebrating your new job. They’ve already ordered a cake.
In the evening the office manager audits the fridge and posts photos of “unclaimed” food. Among them: your grandma’s jar of jam.
You notice the coffee machine was left on for the weekend. Only the office manager has the kitchen key, and she’s already left.
Heading home, you find someone’s forgotten car keys in the kitchen. The keychain has a photo of a dog.
You’re printing handouts for a morning meeting when the printer pops and starts smoking. The office is nearly empty.
At 9 p.m. your manager sends you a seven-minute voice message. The app shows you’ve “listened” to it.
You spent three hours choosing what to wear to tomorrow’s meeting with sales. Your closet holds the same thing in different colors.
An evening email from HR: “Your probation has been successfully extended.” The word “successfully” is especially worrying.
As you leave, you see every monitor in the open space is on and the lights are blazing. The last people left an hour ago.
Dasha greets you at the door: it’s the department head’s birthday, and everyone has signed the card except you. He’ll be here in five minutes.
At stand-up the department head calls you by the previous employee’s name. Second time this week. Everyone acts like it’s normal.
Zhenya offers to drive you to work every morning. The only catch: leaving at 6:50 and listening to investing podcasts.
Irina from accounting calls at 8:45: your bank details had a typo, and your salary went “somewhere.” Today is payday.
left: Go to the bank before work

text: The guard insists you leave your bike outside the premises. There are no racks, just a pole with a “No Parking” sign.
On the bus you see a coworker you didn’t recognize in his winter hat. He says hi, and you stare at him like a stranger.
Leaving home, you find someone has locked the building’s front door from inside. No concierge, and the neighbors are asleep.
An announcement: your transfer station is closed for repairs starting today. You read about it a month ago and forgot.
Kirill from IT says your laptop “arrived, but without a charger.” The charger arrives Thursday. Battery: 18%.
Every morning at nine Tamara opens the window “for fresh air,” then leaves for tea. Today it’s 5°F outside.
Misha the intern came to work in a three-piece suit with a briefcase. You’re in a hoodie. He looks at you with a hint of superiority.
You try making a cappuccino on the professional coffee machine for the first time. There’s foam everywhere except the cup.
There’s a note on your container in the fridge: “Dear sir or madam! Your lunch smells up the whole kitchen. Respectfully, the Kitchen.”
The department cooler dispenses plastic-flavored water and sometimes burps bubbles. Coworkers adore it and call it “Fluffy.”
The department printer is nicknamed “Diva,” and everyone has their own ritual phrase for it. You don’t have yours yet, and you need a printout urgently.
You’re fifteen minutes late because of traffic. In the elevator you bump into the department head, who’s twenty minutes late.
The sales team invited you to a “client lunch” to watch the pros at work. It’s going on three hours, and the client is talking about fishing.
Pavel asks you to cover for him: “If anyone asks, I’m in a meeting.” He’s actually at the barber across the street.
At lunch Lida shows photos of her home renovation — 214 of them. At photo 30 you realize you’re expected to comment on each one.
The group lead asks you to prepare “a little presentation, a couple of slides.” An hour later you learn it’s going to the board of directors.
right: Keep it to a couple slides

text: A courier brings five pizzas someone ordered and asks you to sign. Whoever ordered them isn’t in, and the pizzas are getting cold.
You ordered a “light salad” for lunch, and they brought a bowl the size of a tire. Coworkers are waiting for you to finish.
The cafeteria is full except for the table where the entire senior management is eating. Tray in hand, soup getting cold.
There’s a cold war in the kitchen: someone keeps putting the kettle back empty. You just used it, and it’s empty.
right: Post about it in the chat

text: The coffee machine jammed and wants a service code. The code is on a sticky note behind the machine, high up near the ceiling.
You need a copy of your passport for HR. The copier mirrors everything, and your passport looks like a spy’s.
During your presentation the projector gives the slides a strong blue tint. You’re talking about “warm” leads.
You forgot to mute messenger notifications. Your desk dings every seven seconds, and the open space is getting annoyed.
Your desk neighbor chews his nails during calls. You can hear it even through your headphones.
You wore new shoes, and by lunch you’ve got a blister the size of a coin. Up next: a standing meeting — a warehouse tour with a client.
Making the rounds, your manager notices a job site open on your screen. You were just checking salaries “for general knowledge.”
Your mentor Igor shows you a “secret way” around the approval system. It’s clearly against the rules but saves three days.
The department head asked you to take meeting notes. He talks fast, jumps between topics and suddenly asks: “Got all that?”
At 6 p.m. Roma invites you to play soccer with coworkers. You haven’t played since school, but they need a goalkeeper.
In the evening Ksyusha offers to swap desks: hers is by the window, yours is by the water cooler. She says the cooler is “cozier.”
Alyona from HR writes at 7:30 p.m.: “We need your photo for the newbie board by 9:00 tomorrow — a smiley one.” You’re in pajamas.
You stayed late, and the CEO ends up in the elevator with you. He unexpectedly offers you a lift to the subway.
The evening train is delayed forty minutes. On the platform you meet three coworkers who are also waiting.
right: Wait off to the side with a book

text: You’re sharing a taxi with a coworker. The driver goes through downtown, your coworker says nothing, the meter keeps running. You’re splitting it.
Traffic leaving the city is at a dead stop. The GPS says 2 hours 15 minutes. A coworker is snoring in the back seat.
You were late to your own end-of-probation party: stuck in the elevator. Coworkers already ate the cake.
After the party the fridge holds three salads and half a jar of pickles. The office manager says: “Help yourselves.”
Before leaving you find an unlabeled box of chocolates in the kitchen. The lid says “Help yourself.” Inside: nothing.
left: Bring a box of your own

text: The department ran out of coffee in the evening, and you have three hours of work left. A coworker offers “an energy drink from the stash.” It glows green.
Just before probation ends you get an email: “Complete a self-assessment on 40 criteria.” Due tomorrow morning.
On Friday evening your mentor Igor sends you “some useful weekend reading” — a 600-page book about sales.
All day you were too shy to ask how the coffee machine works, so you drank water. Tomorrow it’ll be the same coffee machine.
Mom asks if anyone’s being mean to you at work. And whether you’d like her to call your boss.
Tomorrow is “White Top, Black Bottom Day.” You own white pants and a black T-shirt. The other way around.
Someone in the newbie chat proposes an “informal meetup” at a bar on Friday. He’s already picked a bar on the other side of town.
Gleb tells you there’s an “unspoken queue” for the best mug in the kitchen. You took it yesterday, not knowing the rules.
Grandma packed you pies for work, one for each person in the department. There are twelve people and seven pies.
Your neighbor across the landing heard you got an office job and asks you to print forty pages of a gardening magazine at work.
At the entrance you’re asked to show what’s in your bag: three bananas, a charger and a pack of cookies “for the team.”
You’re face to face on the subway with someone who clearly had garlic for breakfast. Nowhere to move, six stops to go.
left: Switch cars at the next stop

text: A coworker from accounting is pedaling slowly ahead of you in the bike lane on a cruiser with a basket. No room to pass.
At 8:58 the department head asks why you’re not at your desk. You’re at the coffee machine; there are two minutes till nine.
Sonya brings her kid to the office: the daycare is quarantined. The kid is already at your desk drawing in your planner.
You set your clock fifteen minutes fast so you won’t be late. Now every morning you spend fifteen minutes calculating what time it really is.
left: Set it back to real time

text: Kirill comes to install your antivirus and sees 140 files named “New Document” on your desktop. He silently takes a photo.
left: Ask him not to share it

text: The CEO’s assistant asks you to collect the mail from the ground-floor box every morning, “since you’re the newbie and walk past anyway.”
You got a task, but didn’t understand a word of it. Asking means admitting it. And there are two months of probation left.
You walked into stand-up late just as the boss was saying: “How nice that everyone’s on time.”
Someone left a cup of yesterday’s half-finished latte in the coffee machine. You can’t remove it — it’s stuck.
The department introduced “Green Thursday”: everyone wears all green. It’s Thursday. The only green thing you own is an apple.
left: Put the apple in your pocket

text: A sign on the copy room door: “Printing for business purposes only. Usage is tracked.” You need to print concert tickets.
Over lunch Vadim says he’s been here nine years and “never once taken a vacation.” He gives you a meaningful look.
Alyona from HR invites you for “coffee with HR” to see how you’re settling in. The coffee is instant; the conversation is on the record.
Irina asks you for a signed expense report, though you haven’t spent anything. She says “that’s the rule for newbies.”
At lunch Gosha dares you to eat “the spiciest soup in town.” The loser cleans the coffee machine for a week.
Zlata asks if she can “just for a minute” put her shoe boxes in your desk drawer. Your drawer is small as it is.
The department head asks you to accompany a visiting partner to lunch. The guest speaks only Spanish; yours is “with a dictionary.”
You need to send a letter by courier, but the order form has forty fields, including “letter weight in grams” and “envelope color.”
right: Take it to the post office

text: Your first time changing the cooler jug, and water gushes all over the floor. The cleaner is out at lunch.
Fridays are “fish day” in the cafeteria. On those days the whole department eats at the cafe across the street. You’ve been invited for the first time.
You come back from lunch to find a courier in your chair who’s “just waiting.” He’s been waiting twenty minutes.
Someone hung a poster in the kitchen: “Your mom doesn’t work here.” Under it sits a dirty plate, and everyone’s looking at you.
Your open-space neighbor suggests putting “some greenery for good vibes” on your desk — four pots of basil. It smells like pizza.
The coworker across the desk loudly cracks his neck every half hour. You flinch every time and lose your train of thought.
Your mentor Igor had you reply to a client, but rewrote the whole email in his own words before sending. He cc’d the boss.
Your laptop starts updating in the middle of screen-sharing at a meeting. Update 1 of 27.
At a client meeting a button pops off your blazer and rolls loudly under the conference table. The client watches it closely.
Your manager asks you to draw up your own probation plan. Nobody has told you any goals or criteria yet.
Before leaving, Oleg asks you to “keep an eye on his fish” in the tank by his desk. Feeding is “by eye.” He’s away for a week.
right: Hand it off to the cleaner

text: At 6:30 p.m. Dasha says everyone’s going to trivia night and “you’re coming, right?” The team is called “Office Plankton.”
In the evening HR sends all newbies a 45-minute video address from the CEO, asking for “feedback.”
You boarded the wrong train: it runs nonstop to the end of the line, which is in the next region.
You doze off on the evening bus and drop your phone. In the morning you learn the work chat received the message “aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa.”
You were late for dinner with your parents because you “had to finish something.” Mom has already cleared the table.
At 6:40 p.m. the department head says: “Great job, go home.” Five minutes later he sends a task “for tomorrow morning, but today would be better.”
You left a container of soup in the fridge on Friday. It’s Monday, and coworkers say “something lives in there.”
After you left, someone wrote on your mug in marker: “Longest Coffee Line.” It’s about how long you spend at the machine.
The office manager asks you to learn to take apart the coffee machine “so there’s one more person in charge.” The manual is in Italian.
Your roommate wants help assembling a wardrobe tonight. You’re still at work, and he says “the wardrobe won’t wait.”
Friends invite you to a party celebrating your new job. They’re heading out at 10 p.m.; you have to get up at 6:30.
You arrive at the company evening in a suit, and it turns out to be a pajama party. Everyone’s in slippers with pillows.
Finally the news: you passed probation! The boss suggests celebrating with a department dinner on you.
In the evening the printer suddenly starts printing your college term paper from three years ago. Someone sent it from your account.
All evening you keep remembering calling your boss “Mom” at stand-up. He pretended not to hear.
In the evening team chat, coworkers started a pet photo contest. All you have is a cactus.
Every morning Liza holds “five minutes of positivity”: everyone takes turns saying what they’re grateful for. You’re only grateful the coffee machine works.
Fyodor took over your desk for the morning: “Your monitor’s bigger, and I need to look at some charts.” You came to work, and he’s already there.
left: Let him, sit next to him

text: The department head says to “pick a task from the backlog yourself.” The backlog has 600 tasks, half with no description.
The receptionist asks you to “cover for ten minutes.” Half an hour later she still isn’t back, and the phone is ringing off the hook.
The company system notifies you: “Your password expires in 1 day.” To change it you must call IT, and IT opens at 10:00.
A courier delivered your online order to the office. The box is huge and says “Fragile: Inflatable Pool.” Everyone sees it.
The tram is so slow an old man walking his dog is overtaking it. Four more stops to the office.
First time using car sharing to get to the office, and you can’t find the headlight switch. It’s already light, but the manual mentions a fine.
It’s pouring this morning, and you left your umbrella at the office yesterday. Ten minutes’ walk to the subway, and a 9:30 meeting with your manager.
right: Wait for it to ease up

text: Someone left a note on your yogurt in the fridge: “Not mine, but I really want it.” The yogurt is untouched.
The kitchen dishwasher broke, and the office manager announces: “We wash by hand, in turns.” Newbies go first.
The coffee machine switched to “winter mode” and only dispenses coffee at 9:00, 12:00 and 3:00. It’s 9:03.
The open space got a “thank-you board,” and everyone’s writing sticky notes to each other. Nobody has written one for you yet.
left: Write a note for a coworker

text: An email: “Please log your start and end times daily.” They forgot to install the time-tracking system for you.
You’re summoned to a “partner meeting” in five minutes. You’re wearing a hoodie and sneakers.
You’re running late, and a coworker texts: “No rush, the boss isn’t in yet.” A minute later the boss writes: “Where is everyone?”
Vika asks how you get everything done so fast. You honestly say you use templates — and now Vika wants all of them.
At lunch Arseny holds a tasting of his homemade pickles. The cucumbers, he says, have “a secret ingredient.” The secret smells strong.
Once an hour Lyova stops by your desk: “So, how’s it going?” He just walks on and doesn’t wait for an answer.
The CEO walks past your desk and suddenly asks: “What are you working on right now?” You’re picking lunch in a delivery app.
The printer printed your department budget table in 12-point font across 87 pages. It “forgot” your “fit to one page” setting.
The printer on your floor starts printing by itself — pages of static. Coworkers whisper that “it’s possessed.”
right: Hang a holy icon on it

text: You answered a client’s call, but there are two more voices on the line, all talking at once. Looks like you started a conference call by accident.
At lunch you find a cozy, quiet cafe none of your coworkers know about. Today Lida spots you there and waves happily.
At lunch someone at the next table asks: “Is that your bag in the aisle?” It is, and a serving cart just rolled over it.
You put a cake in the fridge for the department. An hour later half of it is gone, and the party is at 4 p.m.
The coffee machine went on strike, and coworkers have gathered around it for an “emergency meeting.” The department head is waiting for you.
You finally got noise-canceling headphones. Now you can’t hear when people talk to you, and coworkers keep tapping your shoulder.
Someone put up holiday string lights in the open space, blinking right into your eyes. The whole department loves them.
Your mentor Igor says you’re “ready to work independently” and moves to another department. You still have seven questions in your notebook.
In a one-on-one your manager asks: “How do you like it here? Be honest.” The door is closed behind you, his smile is in front of you.
A coworker points out you’re wearing the same cardigan as her. It’s the third time this month she’s joked about “the twins department.”
At 6 p.m. Rita suggests “quickly settling a debate”: the department can’t decide where to hold the New Year’s party. 400 messages in the chat.
Timur asks to borrow your pass: he left his at home and has to come in early tomorrow.
The department head asks why you’re always first to leave. You leave at 6:00, as your contract says.
You’ve been waiting forty minutes for the bus. The board has said “Arriving” the whole time. Coworkers left by taxi long ago.
On the subway you see an ad for a course: “Pass Probation in 3 Days.” Your boss is in the same car.
left: Snap a photo of the ad

text: You’re stuck in traffic, and a company-paid online course starts at 7 p.m. The boss personally asked about your progress.
Late in the kitchen you catch a coworker secretly eating someone else’s candy from a cupboard. He sees you and holds out a piece.
Management decided to move the kitchen coffee machine into the CEO’s office. Coworkers are collecting signatures: “Bring Back the Coffee.”
You stayed late and you’re starving. In the fridge is someone’s labeled chocolate bar. The owner has gone home.
left: Eat it, buy a new one

text: You’re asked to stay late to help with the department move. They promise it’ll “be taken into account” in your probation review.
You were late to a friend’s birthday because you stayed late at work. Your friend says “No big deal,” but sounds hurt.
Tomorrow is “Business Attire Day,” and you’re ironing a shirt. The iron burns an iron-shaped hole in the back.
You get home and realize you’ve walked around all day with a “Don’t forget!” sticky note on your back. Don’t forget what — unknown.
As you fall asleep you remember you never replied to HR’s email about the trial review. It was due today.
A friend calls and asks if your office really has a coffee machine and a foosball table like on TV. All it has is a broken water cooler.
News on the company portal: “Our newbie set a record for fastest onboarding.” It’s you — because you fast-forwarded everything.
In the evening chat coworkers decided you’re in charge of picking the film for “movie night.” The vote is in an hour.
Your former mentor Igor calls in the evening to see “how you’re managing without him.” The call lasts forty minutes.
Kira suggests commuting together on the train “so it’s not boring.” Her train is half an hour earlier than yours.
The facilities manager wants you to sign for your equipment: desk, chair, lamp and “one potted cactus.” The cactus is already dead.
Every morning Galina the cleaner moves your keyboard to the edge of the desk and wipes it with alcohol. The keys are starting to stick.
left: Ask her not to touch it

text: A sign at reception reads “Guests register here.” Once again you’re asked to sign in as a guest, though you’ve worked here three weeks.
Your rental scooter refuses to park by the office: “Restricted zone.” The allowed zone is a ten-minute walk away.
right: Ditch it and pay the fine

text: On the escalator you notice your mentor standing in front of you. He’s yawning and clearly trying not to fall asleep.
The AC above your desk has been blowing like a hurricane since morning. Only the department head has the remote, and he’s on vacation.
Your roommate accidentally drank your morning coffee and left a note: “Sorry, it was a strategic decision.”
Someone in the newbie chat writes: “Has anyone figured out what KPI means?” Silence. You haven’t either, but you decide to answer.
Your manager gives you your first serious task and says: “Don’t worry, you’re on probation, mistakes are allowed.” Sounds ominous.
The elevator arrives with five coworkers already in it. You’d make six; the limit is five. Everyone’s looking at you.
The cashier at the shop near the office remembers you and says every morning: “Coffee and a bun again?” Today you wanted a salad.
A pinecone falls on your head in the office courtyard. A second later you realize a squirrel threw it. Coworkers saw and are filming.
In the morning the department head asks: “What were you doing all day yesterday?” You were at a training session he invited you to.
You’re on probation, and “HR — Inspection” signs are appearing on desks. Today they’re inspecting your department.
Misha the intern asks how to become “a pro like you.” It’s flattering, but you’ve only been at the company a month.
Nina offers to “swap tasks”: hers is “reconcile spreadsheets,” yours is “welcome the delegation.” The delegation brings gifts.
At lunch Stepan confesses your predecessor quit “because of the coffee machine.” He gives no details, just chews meaningfully.
Marketing asks you to star in an ad about “happy employees.” You need to smile and say “I love Mondays.”
The company lawyer asks you to sign a nondisclosure agreement. You don’t know a single company secret yet.
IT support needs a screenshot of the error, or they won’t accept the ticket. The error is that your monitor won’t turn on at all.
Vadim asks you to help move his desk “a couple of inches.” It’s solid oak and weighs as much as a grand piano.
You ordered the business lunch and dipped your sleeve in the soup. In twenty minutes you meet the division director.
The cafeteria cashier won’t take anything bigger than a $20. All you have is a $100 bill, and the line stretches to the door.
The food delivery guy calls: “I’m at the turnstile, they won’t let me in.” You’re on the ninth floor, and the elevator’s under repair.
At lunchtime the coffee machine displays “Error 404: Coffee Not Found.” Someone set it up as a joke. Coworkers are laughing; you want to sleep.
The office manager introduced color-coded stickers by department for fridge food. Your department is pink. There are no stickers.
The printer stamps “Trial Version” in the corner of your documents. The driver license has expired.
The coworker across from you turned her monitor so you can see her chat. They’re discussing your last report, and not kindly.
You’re presenting at a meeting for the first time, but your mic isn’t working online. You’re moving your lips, and the boss says: “Great, thanks!”
Halfway through probation you realize you’ve never seen your own job description. Turns out it’s still “being written.”
You were called into a meeting with investors, but today you came in shorts — it was hot. A coworker’s blazer is three sizes too big for you.
After lunch you were stuck in the elevator for fifteen minutes and missed a call with a client. He thinks you ignored him.
Kira invites you to the department’s “get-to-know-you night”: bowling with team shirts. The shirts are already ordered with your name. Misspelled.
The department head offers you a ride home. On the way he quizzes you: “So what is a profit margin?”
right: Ask to be dropped at the subway

text: You’re leaving at 8 p.m., and the guard says: “Last one out again. Careful, you’ll burn out before probation ends.” He seems to be the only one who noticed.
The taxi driver learns you work in an office and spends the ride urging you to “get out while you’re young.” He’s had three office jobs and a nervous twitch.
Someone offers you their seat on the evening train. You wonder if you really look that tired. They’re waiting for an answer.
Riding your scooter home, you see a coworker walking in the rain. The scooter only fits one.
Late in the kitchen you catch the facilities manager counting tea bags. He looks up: “Was it you who took two?”
You find your lunch in the fridge, a third of it eaten. A note on the container: “Thanks, delicious, can I get the recipe?”
For the first time you’re alone in the office in the evening, and the coffee machine suddenly speaks: “Time to rest.” Must be an update.
The evening office party’s dress code is “Movie Stars.” You came in normal clothes; the boss came as a vampire.
right: Take photos off to the side

text: On the last day of probation HR calls: “We’re still thinking. Come in tomorrow.” Sounds mysterious.
You were late to a school reunion — “work ran late.” Everyone’s already discussing their promotions.
Mom sent you a photo of pies with the caption “Are you eating enough?” — in the work messenger. (How did she get in there?) The whole department sees it.
Your mentor calls in the evening and suggests skipping work tomorrow for an industry expo. The boss doesn’t know yet.
Lying in bed, you realize today might have been the first time in a month you arrived on time. Nobody noticed.
Your roommate asks why you talk in your sleep about “approvals” every night. He recorded it.
In the evening chat coworkers ask: “Who’s bringing something for tea tomorrow?” An awkward pause. You’re the newbie, and everyone’s waiting.
Every morning Dima puts a bowl of candy on the shared table and notes in a notebook who took how many. At month’s end — “the final tally.”
Polina asks you to answer her work phone until lunch because “calls give her migraines.” Your own phone rings just as much.
The HR director does a morning round, asking each newbie: “What animal do you feel like on the team?”
The mail carrier brings a registered letter for you to the office: a fine for riding the train without a ticket. You definitely paid.
First time driving in, you took an empty spot by the entrance. A minute later you learn it’s the CEO’s spot.
Your manager calls while you’re on the bus. The driver just cranked up the music, and the woman next to you is telling a friend about a wedding.
It’s icy this morning, and you arrive at the office having slid the last hundred yards on your soles. Coworkers at the window applaud.
Kirill says your laptop is “infected” and must be reinstalled. All your files from the past week will be gone.
left: Back up to a flash drive

text: Your mentor sends a morning list of “things to know about coworkers”: who loves sweets, who can’t stand loud laughter, who’s “not a morning person.”
You’re handed the key to the safe with the company stamps because “there’s nobody else.” It’s your second week, and there are nine stamps in there.
Someone stuck a note on the coffee machine: “Limit: 2 cups per person per day.” You’re on your third, and the note’s author is standing right there.
You go to put your lunch in the fridge, but it’s so full the door won’t close. On top sits a cake marked “Do Not Touch.”
The department printer now only works through a phone app. The app wants you to accept 47 terms and conditions.
Your desk neighbor is trying to talk you into switching to standing desks together. “They say it’s healthy.” It costs twice as much as a regular desk.
You were late because of roadwork and invented an excuse on the way. But your manager is on vacation, and the deputy didn’t even ask.
Everyone came to work in the same blue sweater: turns out it was a company gift, and you never got one.
In the morning chat a coworker asks: “Who can cover for me on a client call in five minutes?” Silence. Everyone’s waiting for you.
Anatoly, a department veteran, tells you over lunch “how things were back in 2009.” Lunch ended long ago, and he’s only up to 2011.
Zlata brings her dog to the office, and it immediately lies down on your feet. You can’t get up, and there’s a meeting in five minutes.
Internal audit picks you for a “knowledge of procedures” check. The only procedure you’ve read is the one for the coffee machine.
A client calls demanding “that manager who was here before you.” That manager was fired for rudeness.
The cafeteria cook recognizes you and serves soup “home-style, extra big.” The portion is bigger than the bowl. You have a report after lunch.
You’ve noticed the whole department lunches together at 1:00 sharp. You’re used to eating at noon, and your stomach is already protesting.
At lunch a coworker shares something shady about the boss and adds: “Don’t tell anyone!” The boss is sitting at the next table.
A kitchen dispute erupts: put dirty spoons in the sink or wash them right away? You’re asked to be the “impartial judge.”
You find a container in the fridge labeled “Boss’s Lunch. Do Not Open.” It’s sitting on top of your yogurt.
The office bought a new touchscreen coffee machine. Only the IT department knows how to use it, and they’re at lunch.
The meeting-room projector is dead, and the boss asks you to “come up with something.” All you have is a white wall and a laptop.
left: Turn the laptop to the room
right: Run to storage for a projector

text: Open-space neighbors are loudly discussing a show and spoiling the episode you haven’t seen yet. The one you’ve waited for all week.
left: Ask them not to spoil it

text: It’s “Tie Day,” and someone ceremoniously tied a fish-shaped tie on you. Meeting with investors in an hour.
right: Take it off before the meeting

text: Your manager offers to “end your probation early” if you close a task in a week that the last three newbies failed to close.
You were late to your own HR meeting, and HR already left for the next one. Your calendar now says “Meeting missed due to employee.”
At 6 p.m. Yana says it’s her last day and throws a farewell with cake. You’ve known her three days, but the cake looks tempting.
Marat asks you to “babysit” his online presentation tonight: just click “next” on his signal. The signal is his cough.
At 7 p.m. the CEO walks through the office and sees you alone in the open space. He nods and says: “Good.” Unclear what exactly.
On the train you notice the man next to you has a report from your company on his lap stamped “Confidential.” He’s asleep.
Your first rush-hour ride home, and you can’t get off at your stop: the human tide sweeps you back into the car.
You decided to walk home to save money. Halfway there it starts pouring, and your umbrella is at work.
You were late to your own surprise dinner, thrown by coworkers for your first month. Everyone hid for forty minutes.
In the evening you accidentally pressed “Full Cleaning” on the coffee machine. It’ll take two hours and it’s humming through the whole kitchen.
Before the weekend the office manager asks everyone to take their food out of the fridge. Your container is in there, but inside is something you don’t remember.
On your way out you notice someone left the kettle on with nothing in it. It’s starting to smoke.
left: Turn it off, air it out

text: In the evening HR sends a 50-page “business style guide.” Page 12 shows a photo of the shoes you wore today, as an example of “don’t.”
An evening email: “Congratulations on passing probation!” A minute later: “Sorry, this email was sent in error.”
Your mentor suggests continuing “mentorship” over dinners on Fridays. He’s already booked a restaurant.
Friends in the group chat ask why you’ve stopped going out in the evenings. You check the time: 9:40 p.m., and you’ve just left the office.
Friday evening. Your first month at the new job is behind you. You survived, but a coworker already said “next month gets more interesting.”

Your neighbor across the landing heard you work in an office and asks you to “print a couple of photos” at work. A couple means 300.
